extracted.intended_audience: Patent attorneys and agents registered to practice before the USPTO (IP practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for professional conduct of patent attorneys and agents before the USPTO, focusing on avoiding Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) grievances and steps to take if a grievance is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for regulation of practitioner conduct (35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct of patent attorneys and agents is subject to regulation by the USPTO under 35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2)(D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may establish regulations, not inconsistent with law, which may govern the conduct of agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the Office. See Lacavera v. Dudas, 441 F.3d 1380 (Fed. Cir. 2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for discipline (35 U.S.C. §32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may, after notice and opportunity for a hearing, suspend or exclude from further practice any person shown to be incompetent or disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or who does not comply with regulations under section 2(b)(2)(D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO may discipline individuals for misconduct related to service, advice, and assistance in prosecution or prospective prosecution of applications. See Bender v. Dudas, 490 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2007). Discipline applies regardless of whether conduct was related to patent or trademark prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 1 — Maintain integrity and competence of the legal profession
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should assist in maintaining the integrity and competence of the legal profession. (37 C.F.R. §10.21)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General normative standard: actions should support overall integrity and competence of the profession; referenced as foundational when avoiding grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 2 — Make legal counsel available
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should assist the legal profession in fulfilling its duty to make legal counsel available. (37 C.F.R. §10.30)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be mindful of access considerations when advising and serving clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 3 — Prevent unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should assist in preventing the unauthorized practice of law. (37 C.F.R. §10.46)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid aiding nonlawyers or unauthorized persons to perform legal services; recent disciplinary actions include aiding unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 4 — Preserve client confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should preserve the confidences of the client. (37 C.F.R. §10.56)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to grievances, practitioners must still respect client confidences; confidentiality is a central ethical obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 5 — Exercise independent professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should exercise independent professional judgment on behalf of a client. (37 C.F.R. §10.61)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advising clients requires independent judgment; do not let conflicts or improper influences override professional judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 6 — Represent a client competently
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should represent a client competently. (37 C.F.R. §10.76)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes meeting deadlines, proper prosecution, and technical/legal knowledge; incompetence is a ground for discipline under 35 U.S.C. §32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 7 — Represent zealously within bounds of law
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should represent a client zealously within the bounds of the law. (37 C.F.R. §10.83)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zealous representation must still comply with legal and ethical constraints; frivolous appeals and improper conduct can lead to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 8 — Assist in improving the legal system
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should assist in improving the legal system. (37 C.F.R. §10.100)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional conduct should contribute positively to the functioning and improvement of the legal process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon 9 — Avoid appearance of impropriety
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should avoid even the appearance of professional impropriety. (37 C.F.R. §10.110)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be conscious not only of actual impropriety but also situations that could reasonably be perceived as improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect (frequent cause of grievances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect in client matters is a common basis for grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: failure or delay in filing patent application; failure to reply to Office actions; failure to revive or assist in reviving abandoned applications; failure to turn over files to new representative; failure to communicate with client; failing to report Office actions; failing to reply to client inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, Fraud, Deceit or Misrepresentation (lack of candor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of candor with clients or USPTO (dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation) is a major grievance category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: concealing date of Office action, abandonment, and true reason for abandonment from client; misrepresenting status of abandoned application; making false statements to USPTO in petitions for extension of time; adjudication of inequitable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returned payments and commingling of funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial mishandling including returned payments and commingling client funds frequently leads to grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: checks returned or EFTs dishonored for insufficient funds; repeated failure to reply to notices of missing filing fees; check kiting; failure to return client’s advanced fees; improper commingling of clients’ advanced fees with practitioner’s funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. §11.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners disciplined in another jurisdiction may be subject to reciprocal discipline by the USPTO; obligations and procedures are set out in 37 C.F.R. §11.24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within 30 days of disbarment/suspension/reprimand/probation or disciplinary disqualification elsewhere, a practitioner must notify the OED Director in writing. OED will obtain certified record and file a complaint complying with 37 C.F.R. §11.34. USPTO Director generally imposes identical discipline unless practitioner clearly and convincingly shows: (i) lack of due process elsewhere, (ii) infirmity of proof, or (iii) imposition of identical discipline would result in grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievances against practitioners originate from multiple sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External to USPTO: clients, colleagues, others. Internally within USPTO: Patent Corps, Trademark Corps, others. Other sources: case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance lifecycle / OED process
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedural path a grievance follows at OED from receipt to potential referral to Committee on Discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flow: OED receives information → decide whether to investigate → if yes, conduct investigation → form opinion whether violation occurred → close matter or file complaint → if complaint filed, determine probable cause → if probable cause, refer to Committee on Discipline (and potentially further proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to respond if you receive a grievance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical steps practitioners should take upon receiving a grievance from OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly; when appropriate, provide supporting documents; respect client confidences; do not bill the client for responding to the grievance. Be mindful that responses and supporting material can affect outcomes (dismissals, warnings, or disciplinary action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of misconduct recently disciplined (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative categories of conduct that have led to public discipline by OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples: false representations (ownership of application; abandonment of application(s)); duty of disclosure — related litigation; payments from invention development companies; aiding unauthorized practice of law; returned payments & insufficient funds; improper commingling of funds; failure to file applications; document fabrication — false docketing; undisclosed conflicting interest in attorney’s ownership of search service; non-itemized invoices; unaccounted costs; frivolous appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to disciplinary decisions (transparency / precedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions imposing public discipline are available for review via the FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette for Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FOIA Reading Room: http://des.uspto.gov/Foia/OEDReadingRoom.jsp (select 'Discipline' in Decision Type and click 'Get Info'). Official Gazette for Patents: http://www.uspto.gov/news/og/patent_og/index.jsp (select issue and 'Notices'). Use these resources to review precedent and understand sanction patterns.
